evidence: They emit ultrasonic calls through their larynx and process the returning echoes to build a three-dimensional acoustic image of their surroundings.
The FM sweep provides range resolution through the time-bandwidth product: the wider the bandwidth and the shorter the duration, the finer the range resolution.
As a bat approaches prey, it progressively shortens its calls.
The bat measures the echo delay (which gives target range) and adjusts its next call's duration accordingly.
These bats emit a long-duration call at a specific frequency and listen for Doppler shifts in the echo caused by their own flight speed and the target's movement.
The auditory system has a specialized 'acoustic fovea' — a region of the cochlea tuned to a narrow frequency band around the call frequency — that provides extreme sensitivity to frequency shifts.

To keep the echo within this acoustic fovea, horseshoe bats perform Doppler-shift compensation: they lower their call frequency as they fly faster, so that the Doppler-shifted echo remains at the foveal frequency.
Bats process echoes using a combination of spectral and temporal features. The FM sweep creates a 'spectrogram' that encodes target shape and texture.
The auditory processing involves specialized neurons that are tuned to specific combinations of frequency and timing, effectively performing a matched-filter operation on the echo.
The FM sweep creates a 'spectrogram' that encodes target shape and texture: different frequencies reflect differently from different surface geometries, creating a spectral signature.
Range ambiguity: When target range exceeds the call duration times the speed of sound, the echo from one call arrives during the next call, creating range ambiguity.
Clutter interference: In dense vegetation, echoes from background objects (leaves, branches) can mask target echoes.
Frequency-dependent attenuation: High frequencies attenuate faster in air, limiting the detection range for high-frequency calls.

Interference from conspecifics: In large colonies, the jamming avoidance response may be insufficient, and bats may experience degraded performance due to acoustic interference from many simultaneous callers.
The bat measures the echo delay (which gives target range) and adjusts its next call's duration accordingly.
Bats dynamically adjust their call duration based on the distance to the target. As a bat approaches prey, it progressively shortens its calls.
